Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician and writer. In 1843 she described a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers using Babbage's Analytical Engine. This is why she is often called the first programmer. In today's terms: she wrote software for a computer that did not yet exist. Courage? Yes. Compatibility? Scheduled for later. History without our embellishments ↗ 1815 Hello, world. She was born on 10 December in London. Her father was the poet Lord Byron. Poetry in her DNA. Logic on the roadmap. 1833 Networking with destiny. She met Charles Babbage and learned about his work on calculating machines. The best meetup without name badges. 1843 A note that made history. She added seven extensive notes to her translation of Menabrea's article. “I only added a few little things.” ∞ A legacy with no expiry date. She saw the machine's potential beyond ordinary calculation. We are still battling the printer. Editor's note: The biographical facts are real. The jokes are ours. This CV is a creative tribute, not an actual job application. CURRICULUM VITAE / AN ALTERNATE PRESENT № 1843 Programmer & analyst I turn complex briefs into precise steps. Technical documentation worth reading. Connecting mathematics, creativity and practical questions. Patience with hardware. Historically proven. title: Historical sources and books
description: Verified historical sources, Ada's notes, mathematical letters and three real books. Archives, interpretation and fiction are clearly distinguished.
text: SALON / A LIBRARY WITHOUT INVENTIONS 04 / A LIBRARY WITHOUT INVENTIONS Trust us. But open the source. We like humour. We like citations even more. This is where our Steam Cloud ends and real letters, archives and books begin. A -G PRIMARY SOURCES SCHOLARLY CONTEXT REAL BOOKS Straight from Ada. Almost without an intermediary. The historical texts are in English. Links open on the original websites. 01 ORIGINAL TEXT · 1843 Notes by the Translator Ada's Notes A - G in their historical wording. A direct view of her thinking about the Analytical Engine. An electronic transcription hosted by York University; the text is in English. Read the notes ↗ 02 MANUSCRIPTS & LETTERS Ada Lovelace's mathematical papers Digitised materials and research context from the Clay Mathematics Institute project. A good starting point if you want to know how she learned mathematics. Open the archive ↗ 03 CORRESPONDENCE · 1840 - 1841 Lovelace ↔ De Morgan Letters, transcriptions and specific mathematical questions. Even a pioneer asked when she did not understand something. An excellent argument in favour of asking questions. Explore the letters ↗ WHEN CONTEXT HELPS Science Museum Group An overview of Ada Lovelace's life and work from a museum institution. Read the profile ↗ Computer History Museum Ada, Babbage and the importance of her notes in the history of computing. Read the historical context ↗ University of Oxford Research into Ada's mathematical education and links to scholarly publications. Explore the research ↗ Onto the bookshelf. Not into your bookmarks forever. Three different ways to get to know Ada. Bibliographic details refer to the edition listed. FROM THE SALON LIBRARY 01 Christopher Hollings RESEARCH & BIOGRAPHY Ada Lovelace: The Making of a Computer Scientist Christopher Hollings, Ursula Martin & Adrian Rice Bodleian Library Publishing · 2018 How Ada became a mathematician. Based on archival research, this book follows her education and scientific thinking. About the book at the University of Oxford ↗ FROM THE SALON LIBRARY 02 Benjamin Woolley BIOGRAPHY Ada Lovelace: Bride of Science Benjamin Woolley Pan · 2015 edition A biography set within Ada's family, relationships and the scientific world of her time. Best enjoyed with a large pot of tea. The book at its publisher ↗ FROM THE SALON LIBRARY 03 Sydney Padua COMIC · ALTERNATE HISTORY The Thrilling Adventures of Lovelace and Babbage Sydney Padua Penguin · paperback 2016 A humorous graphic novel with historical notes and invented adventures. Narrative fiction, not a literal biography. The book at its publisher ↗ The colourful book designs are our illustrations, not reproductions of the covers. Links lead to publishers or a university's description of the book. We do not list prices or availability. How to read this website Was she really “the first programmer”? She is often called that, particularly because of her published Note G from 1843. The precise claim to being first depends on what we mean by a program and publication; Babbage also produced earlier unpublished procedures. Her importance lies not just in the headline, but in explaining the machine's wider possibilities. Historical context ↗ What did we invent on this website? TeaScript, Steam Cloud, Salon Undo, the AI beach images, the modern CV, cover letters and all contemporary quips. They are labelled as fiction. We do not attribute invented endorsements or job offers to anyone. Where does the portrait come from? A historical watercolour from around 1840 attributed to Alfred Edward Chalon. The reproduction is listed as public domain on Wikimedia Commons. Origin, attribution and licence ↗ Links and bibliographic details checked on 11 November 2026. Encyclopaedic starting point: Ada Lovelace on Wikipedia ↗ . CONTINUE THROUGH THE SALON Her name lives on in a programming language too. ↗

title: Ask the countess.
description: Ada's fictional programming advice: bugs, AI, deadlines, meetings and learning to code, with Victorian humour.
text: 09 / THE POETICAL SCIENCE ADVICE DESK Ask the countess. Six modern problems. One suspiciously well-prepared lady from the 19th century. Original humorous dialogues, not historical quotations. Answers are written in advance; this is not a live AI conversation. Choose a question for Ada Why does my code not work? Will artificial intelligence replace me? What if I cannot meet the deadline? Must I attend another meeting? How do I learn to program? Can I deploy a change on Friday evening? ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Why does my code not work? Ada might say Dear visitor, my program had to wait for hardware too. Before blaming the universe, check the last line. And the one before it. The universe can wait. Now for the practical advice Reproduce the bug with the smallest possible example. Compare the expected and actual results, then fix one thing at a time. ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Will artificial intelligence replace me? Ada might say It may write you a loop. Someone still needs to work out why you wanted to repeat the same mistake a thousand times. Now for the practical advice Use AI as an assistant. Learn to understand the task, read the resulting code and check how it behaves. ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE What if I cannot meet the deadline? Ada might say Say so before the client starts using yesterday as a delivery date. The Analytical Engine had a complicated schedule too. Now for the practical advice Explain what is finished, what is blocking progress and the realistic next step. Agree on a smaller scope or a new deadline. ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Must I attend another meeting? Ada might say If its only outcome is let's arrange another meeting, I suggest correspondence. It is slower, but at least nobody shares the wrong window. Now for the practical advice Ask for the meeting's purpose and the decision needed. A simple project update can often be sent in writing. ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE How do I learn to program? Ada might say Start with a small problem that interests you. I chose a machine that did not exist yet. You need not copy that part of my approach. Now for the practical advice Build a small project, break it into steps and check the result after each change. Ask why the solution works. ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Can I deploy a change on Friday evening? Ada might say Certainly. One can also pour evening tea into a keyboard. Being technically possible does not make something a good plan. Now for the practical advice Before deploying, check the change, prepare a way back to a working version and agree on who will be available if something goes wrong. title: The Salon Tech Gazette.
description: A fictional Victorian technology newspaper: a steam cloud, meetings by letter and very serious tea troubles.
text: 10 / A NEWSROOM POWERED BY STEAM AND SATIRE The Salon Tech Gazette. The 1843-ish edition. Every story is invented. The editorial outrage is a performance. FICTIONAL EDITION · 1843-ish Everything that never happened, all in one place. ✳ All stories Cloud and machines Salon life Poetical Science Number of stories: 6 Cloud and machines 01 ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Steam Cloud escapes up the chimney again. Customers report data showers. The operator recommends a bucket and a local backup. Read the full article The fictional company Steam Cloud announced today that its infrastructure has moved into the upper atmosphere. The migration was unplanned and caused by a draught. File recovery will resume after the rain. The editors note that ordinary paper may not scale, but it rarely leaves the room through the chimney. Cloud and machines 02 ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Hardware arriving soon, says announcement from 1843. The project plan has three phases: design, waiting and renaming waiting as research. Read the full article Our fictional supplier has unveiled a new order status: almost probably on its way. Meanwhile, programmers are testing on paper, which boasts excellent battery life. This is satire about modern projects, not a real statement by Charles Babbage or a historical news report. Salon life 03 ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Programmer declines meeting that could have been a letter. A request for a clear meeting agenda shakes the salon. A working group has been formed. Read the full article A fictional committee met for two hours to decide whether to meet again tomorrow. The Ada of our alternative reality sent a single paragraph with the solution. The committee praised her initiative and proposed an hour-long presentation of the paragraph. Meanwhile, the butler solved the problem by stopping the tea refills. Salon life 04 ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Bug in machine demands recognition as a feature. It has six legs, no documentation and very strong views on backwards compatibility. Read the full article In our fictional salon, a beetle refuses to move out until it gets its own ticket. It claims that unpredictable results encourage creativity. The editors suggest a safe relocation to the garden and a fix for the program. This story is not a historical account of the origin of the term bug. Poetical Science 05 ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE Research: one biscuit improves reviewer's mood. The study has one participant. He insists on an immediate repeat of the experiment. Read the full article In an entirely fictional experiment, an editor received a biscuit and stopped complaining about semicolons. The researchers draw no scientific conclusions, because the researchers do not exist either. The only reliable finding: the biscuits ran out before the code review comments did. Poetical Science 06 ✳ INVENTED FOR THIS WEBSITE TeaGPT promises a revolution. So far, it predicts the next sip. The fictional model was trained on three tea leaves and one piece of society gossip. Read the full article The fictional service TeaGPT answers every question with it depends on the water temperature. Investors in our imaginary salon are delighted, because the answer works even when asked about the business model. The editors recommend checking claims and drinking ordinary tea without a subscription. AN ADVERTISEMENT WE ALSO MADE UP TeaScript Premium: the same tea, now with an invoice. First sip included in the trial.

text: 11 / Behind the salon doors About the Ada site Programming history, curiosity and humour at the same table. This is the story of a website that even sent Ada Lovelace to the beach with a laptop. Made with ideas, code and a little strong tea. Author and concept creator Photo: VITA ↗ Miroslav Reiter Lecturer · IT specialist · educator Miroslav Reiter is a lecturer and founder of IT Academy and the VITA learning platform. His work focuses on practical education in IT, marketing and management. More about the author on VITA ↗ His research explores digital transformation, gamification and online learning, connecting academic knowledge with practice. title: Ada’s algorithm, step by step
description: Bernoulli numbers without the panic. Advance at your own pace and watch what happens to every fraction.
text: 12 / The learning salon Ada’s algorithm, step by step Bernoulli numbers without the panic. Advance at your own pace and watch what happens to every fraction. B₂ A program before the computer In Note G, published in 1843, Ada described a calculation for Babbage’s proposed Analytical Engine. Her table showed how to calculate a Bernoulli number using earlier values. This is a modern educational visualisation inspired by Note G. It uses a simple recurrence, not an exact simulation of the original machine’s cards and registers. Bernoulli numbers appear, for example, in formulas for sums of powers. Mind the historical labels Ada’s B1, B3, B5 and B7 correspond to today’s B2, B4, B6 and B8. The original table calculated her B7, which is modern B8 = -1/30. Our modern convention uses B0 = 1 and B1 = -1/2. B₁ → B₂ · B₃ → B₄ · B₅ → B₆ · B₇ → B₈ Note G, 1843 ↗ NIST DLMF, 24.2 ↗ A recipe without a steam boiler Take the Bernoulli numbers you already know. For each term, find C(n+1, k), the number of ways to choose k elements from n+1. Multiply each known number by its coefficient and add it to the running total S. Reverse the sign of the total and divide by n+1. The result is the required Bn. The fractions stay exact. The tea may be approximately warm. 01 / Have a go A calculation under the magnifying glass Start with B2. Next step adds one term at a time. Go back, restart or choose a more demanding number. Nothing advances automatically. Which number shall we calculate? B₂ B₄ B₆ B₈ Values we already know These values are inputs to the current calculation. The highlighted term is the one being used. Calculation progress Running total S 0 Previous step Next step Start again The interactive calculation needs JavaScript. Expand the worked B2 example below to read the complete calculation. The complete B2 example B₀ = 1, B₁ = -1/2 S = 1 × 1 + 3 × (-1/2) = -1/2 B₂ = -S / 3 = 1/6 The coefficients are 1 and 3. The total is -1/2. Reversing the sign and dividing by three gives 1/6. title: Women in computing history
description: From symbolic instructions to flight software. Four pioneers whose work helped change what computers could do.
text: 14 / The learning salon Women in computing history From symbolic instructions to flight software. Four pioneers whose work helped change what computers could do. { } Computing history was not made by one genius at a lonely desk. It is also a story of teams, collaboration and women whose work deserves attention. The connections to Ada below are thematic parallels. We do not claim that she directly inspired or personally influenced each of these scientists. GH A-0 · FLOW-MATIC Grace Hopper Grace Hopper developed early compilers and FLOW-MATIC, a language that influenced COBOL. She helped bring programming closer to human language. COBOL was a collaboration between multiple people and organisations. How this story connects to Ada Understandable symbols can represent precise instructions. The bridge between human intention and what a machine can execute matters. Computer History Museum: Grace Hopper ↗ MH Apollo Margaret Hamilton Margaret Hamilton led the team developing flight software for the Apollo programme. Her work included reliability, testing and task priorities. Successful missions depended on many specialists working together. How this story connects to Ada An idea for a calculation is not enough. We need a precise procedure and must consider what happens under unexpected conditions. NASA: Margaret Hamilton ↗ JB ENIAC Jean Bartik Jean Bartik was one of the six original ENIAC programmers. She later helped convert it into a stored-program computer and also worked on BINAC and UNIVAC I. How this story connects to Ada A mathematical problem must be broken into operations a machine can handle. Programming involves more than typing into an editor. Computer History Museum: Jean Bartik ↗ FA IBM · PTRAN Frances Allen Frances Allen researched compiler optimisation and automatic parallel execution. Her work helped programs run more efficiently. She became the first woman to receive the Turing Award, for 2006. How this story connects to Ada The order and organisation of calculations affect performance. Good programming also means finding a more effective procedure. IBM: Frances Allen ↗ A small research mission Choose one person. Use the linked source to find a specific project, collaborators and the problem she tackled. Write three sentences without using “the only one” or “all by herself”. title: Fact or myth?
description: A historical fog detector. Five claims, verifiable sources and a clear distinction between Ada’s words and our jokes.
text: 15 / The learning salon Fact or myth? A historical fog detector. Five claims, verifiable sources and a clear distinction between Ada’s words and our jokes. ?! Make a guess before revealing the explanation. In history, the most honest answer is sometimes “needs context”. 01 Ada was the first programmer. Reveal the explanation and source Needs context She is often described this way in connection with the procedure published in 1843. Her collaboration with Babbage and the originality of individual contributions remain subjects of historical discussion. The title is shorthand, not the whole story. Computer History Museum ↗ 02 She only translated someone else’s article. Reveal the explanation and source Myth She added extensive notes to Menabrea’s article, including a computational procedure. Her published contribution therefore went beyond translation alone. Computer History Museum ↗ 03 She ran her program on a completed Analytical Engine. Reveal the explanation and source Myth The Analytical Engine was not completed during her lifetime. The table in Note G described planned operations, not a record of a successful run on a finished machine. Computer History Museum ↗ 04 She also considered machine-generated music. Reveal the explanation and source Fact She imagined manipulating symbols beyond ordinary arithmetic, provided their relationships could be expressed as rules. Note A mentions the possibility of composing music. Note G, 1843 ↗ 05 Her B7 is today’s seventh Bernoulli number. Reveal the explanation and source Myth Historical B7 in Note G corresponds to modern B8 = -1/30. Modern B7 is zero. Always check the notation when reading old formulas. Note G, 1843 ↗ Verified historical quotation What Ada actually wrote “The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate any thing.” Original English wording, retaining the historical spelling “any thing”. Note G, 1843. She is discussing the Analytical Engine and the instructions we can give it. This quotation alone does not settle debates about modern AI’s capabilities. Note G, 1843 ↗ A fictional line for this website What our salon puts in her mouth Tea first, compiler second. We made up this sentence for fun. It is not a historical Ada Lovelace quotation. Her modern startups and beach coding are fictional too. More sources and books ↗ Explore more of the salon 01 Ada’s algorithm, step by step Bernoulli numbers without the panic. title: Behind the scenes with AI
description: Real requests, real changes and lessons from this website. Even a digital salon needs an editor, testing and the occasional furniture rearrangement.
text: 16 / The learning salon Behind the scenes with AI Real requests, real changes and lessons from this website. Even a digital salon needs an editor, testing and the occasional furniture rearrangement. AI How ideas became a website This website is a collaboration between Miroslav Reiter, ChatGPT and Codex. Successive requests added humour, new pages, five languages, appearance modes and easier mobile controls. Miroslav defines the purpose and requests specific changes. AI helps with design, writing, translation and code. Historical claims need sources, generated images need labels and the result needs human judgement. The examples below are real excerpts from the author’s requests in this chat. We retain the original Slovak wording in every language edition and add a translation or explanation. This is not a complete conversation transcript. Request: give it a spark nech je to vtipné a zábavné ten web Translation: make the website funny and entertaining. Result: historical projects sit alongside TeaScript, a fictional modern CV, a salon advice column and AI beach scenes. Fiction is explicitly labelled. Request: a more compact header daj prepínače jazyka a vzhľadu vedľa seba do hlavičky, nech nezaberajú toľko miesta. Translation: put the language and appearance switches next to each other in the header so they take up less space. Result: language and appearance controls sit side by side. On mobile, the time machine, cards, advice and newspaper links moved into the menu. New learning pages are under Discover. Request: the author’s real photograph Na podstránku O stránke Ada pridaj aj moju fotografiu z webu VITA. Translation: add my photograph from the VITA website to About Ada. Result: About Ada contains the original VITA photograph, screen-reader text and a source link. The author’s portrait was not AI-generated. Before and after the change Real screenshots of earlier Slovak versions show the addition of the author’s photograph. Text inside the screenshots is Slovak; the captions are translated. Before An author card without a photograph. Open the full screenshot After A VITA photograph with its source. Open the full screenshot What we worked through The header took up too much space The author requested more compact controls. Shrinking the text was not enough: we put the switches on one row and moved extra mobile links into the menu. Emoji flags are not dependable everywhere The language picker needed flags that displayed on Windows too. We used separate SVG images alongside the language’s name and code. Visible text must match the accessible name Checks led us to adjust the controls’ screen-reader names so they included the visible language code. Good looks alone are not a sufficient usability check. How we check the result We check links, translation coverage, mobile layouts, keyboard controls and interactive behaviour. Source files and downloadable materials are kept in GitHub. Automated checks do not replace a complete accessibility audit or expert review of every translation. The website does not claim full WCAG certification. Further updates address specific findings. title: Teacher solutions: Ada and algorithms
text: Ada Lovelace · Teachers’ corner Teacher solutions: Ada and algorithms For learners aged about 12 and above, and beginner programmers. No coding experience is needed; basic fraction skills help with the numerical activity. Bring paper, a pen and a device with a web browser. One device per pair or a teacher’s projector is enough. The downloaded worksheet also works offline. Print / save as PDF Name: ____________________  Date: ____________________ 1. A program on paper Start with 2. Add 3, multiply the result by 4 and subtract 1. Record every intermediate value. What changes if you swap the first two instructions? Original order: 2 → 5 → 20 → 19. After swapping addition and multiplication: 2 → 8 → 11 → 10. The order of instructions affects the result. 2. Source detectives Assess this claim: Ada ran her algorithm on a completed Analytical Engine. Find a reliable source, record its title and explain your verdict in one sentence. Myth. The Analytical Engine was not completed during Ada’s lifetime. A suitable source is Computer History Museum, Ada Lovelace, or the historical text and context in Sources. 3. Bernoulli without panic Use B0 = 1 and B1 = -1/2. Calculate S = 1 × B0 + 3 × B1, then B2 = -S / 3. Explain what a running total means. S = 1 - 3/2 = -1/2. B2 = -(-1/2) / 3 = 1/6. A running total stores the sum of the terms processed so far. 4. Improve your program In Punched cards, create a short program using the available instructions. Write down the expected result, run the program and change one instruction. Explain the difference. Without a device, use activity 1 instead. Open activity: assess the prediction, recorded instructions and explanation of the change. There is no single required result. Paper example: changing the final subtraction from 1 to 2 changes 19 to 18. To finish What surprised you? Which claim did you verify? How would you explain an algorithm to someone younger?
